body:
What happens after immediate disaster response?

A disaster may destroy houses, interrupt electricity and drinking-water supplies, damage roads, and prevent people from earning their usual income. Emergency response concentrates on saving lives, providing immediate relief and protecting people from further harm. Once the most urgent needs are addressed, the longer process of disaster recovery becomes increasingly important.

Recovery is the process of restoring or improving livelihoods, health, services, infrastructure and other economic, social, cultural and environmental systems affected by a disaster. It should also reduce vulnerability to future disasters.

Recovery is broader than repairing damaged property. A rebuilt school is of limited use if teachers cannot return, children remain displaced or the road to the school is unusable. Similarly, repairing fishing boats does not fully restore livelihoods if landing facilities and markets remain closed.

Relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction

These activities are connected, but their purposes differ.

ActivityMain purposeIllustration
ReliefMeet immediate survival and basic needs.Temporary shelter, drinking water and emergency food assistance.
RehabilitationRestore basic services and facilities needed for community functioning.Reopening a health centre and restoring essential water supply.
ReconstructionRebuild housing, infrastructure and livelihoods over the medium or long term.Constructing safer permanent houses and restoring damaged roads.
RecoveryRestore or improve the overall functioning and well-being of the affected community.Combining housing, essential services, employment and risk reduction.

These are overlapping processes rather than rigid, separate stages. Temporary repairs may begin while emergency relief continues. Permanent reconstruction may take years, while livelihood support may be needed throughout the recovery period.

The meaning of Build Back Better

Build Back Better (BBB) means using recovery, rehabilitation and reconstruction as opportunities to make communities safer and more resilient than they were before the disaster. The aim is not simply to recreate the conditions that allowed earlier damage to occur.

For example, replacing a flood-damaged house with an equally vulnerable structure in the same exposed location may restore shelter without reducing future risk. A better recovery decision would consider the location, safer construction practices, access to services, affordability and the needs of the household.

Build Back Better applies beyond buildings. It can involve restoring livelihoods through more reliable markets, improving public-service continuity, protecting natural ecosystems and making recovery assistance accessible to vulnerable groups.

The Sendai Framework connection

The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030 identifies 4 priorities for action. Its Priority 4 calls for enhancing disaster preparedness for effective response and building back better during recovery, rehabilitation and reconstruction.

This reflects an important principle: recovery planning should begin before a disaster. Governments and communities can identify likely risks, clarify responsibilities, prepare financing arrangements and establish safer reconstruction standards in advance.

Restoring the past and reducing future risk are different objectives. Recovery may restore a service, but Build Back Better also examines whether that service will withstand future hazards.

Prelims focus

  • The Sendai Framework covers the period 2015–2030.
  • Priority 4 includes preparedness for response and Build Back Better in recovery, rehabilitation and reconstruction.
  • Rehabilitation focuses on restoring basic services and facilities.
  • Reconstruction includes medium- and long-term rebuilding of housing, infrastructure and livelihoods.
  • Build Back Better incorporates disaster risk reduction into recovery.
  • Trap: Recovery is not limited to rebuilding physical infrastructure.

[Sources: United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction, Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030, Priority 4 and paragraphs 32–34 (2015); UNDRR, Sendai Framework Terminology, entries Recovery, Rehabilitation, Reconstruction and Build Back Better (2017). Online sources consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Understanding Recovery and Build Back Better

body:
Why assessment comes before major recovery decisions

Recovery requires decisions about which areas need assistance, which services must be restored first, how much financing is necessary and who is likely to remain vulnerable. These decisions become more reliable when they are based on a systematic assessment of the disaster's effects.

A useful assessment begins with a pre-disaster baseline: the condition of housing, infrastructure, economic activities, public services and vulnerable populations before the event. The post-disaster situation is then compared with this baseline.

Damage, loss and needs are different concepts

ConceptMeaningExample
DamageDirect physical destruction or deterioration of assets caused by the disaster.A cyclone destroys boats, damages a fishing harbour and breaks electrical equipment.
Economic lossChanges in economic flows because production or services are interrupted or become more expensive.Fishing income falls while damaged boats and the harbour remain unusable.
Recovery needsResources and actions required to restore services, livelihoods and assets, including suitable improvements for future safety.Repairing harbour facilities, supporting fishing households and restoring safer electricity infrastructure.

Damage concerns assets; economic loss concerns flows over time. A destroyed shop building is physical damage. The business income that cannot be earned while the shop remains closed is an economic loss. Temporary rental costs or additional expenses needed to continue essential services may also be counted as losses under the assessment methodology.

The term recovery needs is forward-looking. It asks what must be financed and done next. The cost may differ from the estimated damage because reconstruction prices, improved safety measures, service-restoration needs and livelihood assistance must be considered.

Recovery needs are not automatically equal to damage plus losses. The 3 estimates answer different questions. Adding them without examining their definitions, assumptions and possible overlaps can produce misleading figures.

Understanding direct and indirect effects

A disaster often produces a sequence of connected effects. Suppose a coastal fishing community experiences a severe cyclone:

  1. Fishing boats and harbour equipment are damaged.
  2. Fishing trips cannot take place, reducing household income.
  3. Transport and market disruption affect fish traders and other workers.
  4. Households may borrow money, reduce consumption or sell productive assets.
  5. Recovery requires repairs, income restoration and measures to reduce future vulnerability.

The initial physical damage is only one part of this chain. The wider social and economic effects may continue after the immediate hazard has ended.

Post-Disaster Needs Assessment

A Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA) is a coordinated, usually government-led assessment of disaster effects and the requirements for recovery and reconstruction. The methodology developed jointly by the United Nations, World Bank and European Union brings together evidence from multiple sectors.

Assessments commonly consider:

  • Housing and settlements: damaged homes, displacement, access to land and essential services.
  • Infrastructure: transport, electricity, water, communications and public facilities.
  • Productive sectors: agriculture, livestock, fisheries, industry and trade.
  • Social services: health, education and community services.
  • Human impacts: changes in employment, income, access to services, poverty and vulnerability.
  • Recovery priorities: immediate restoration, medium-term rehabilitation and longer-term reconstruction.

A rapid assessment immediately after a disaster usually concentrates on urgent needs and the areas most severely affected. A comprehensive PDNA provides a deeper basis for recovery investment and coordination. The 2 assessments serve different purposes and may be updated as additional information becomes available.

Assessment must include people who are difficult to count

Official records may fail to capture informal workers, tenants, migrants, people without formal property documents, unpaid care work and small enterprises operating outside registration systems. An assessment that counts only registered buildings or formal businesses can therefore underestimate the needs of vulnerable households.

Consultation with affected communities, appropriate disaggregation of information and checks against multiple sources help produce a more inclusive picture. Human deaths, illness, displacement and psychological distress must be documented as serious human impacts; they should not be treated merely as physical-asset losses.

Prelims focus

  • Damage refers principally to physical assets.
  • Economic losses include interrupted production, reduced revenue and additional operating costs.
  • Recovery needs estimate the resources required for restoration and improvement.
  • PDNA examines damage, losses, human impacts and recovery needs across sectors.
  • A comprehensive assessment should consider both physical infrastructure and livelihoods.
  • Trap: A damaged asset and the income lost because that asset cannot be used are not the same category.

[Sources: United Nations Development Programme, Post-Disaster Needs Assessment, overview and joint assessment methodology (22 November 2015); UNDP, Assessment Forms: Post Disaster Needs Assessment Guidelines, overview (1 September 2026); World Bank and partner institutions, Pakistan Floods 2022: Post-Disaster Needs Assessment, methodology and definitions of damage, loss, and recovery and reconstruction needs (2022). Online sources consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Assessing Disaster Damage, Economic Losses and Recovery Needs

body:
Recovery must restore the functions of a community

Houses, roads, water systems, electricity networks, health facilities and economic activities are interconnected. A community may have permanent houses but still struggle to recover if drinking water is unsafe, transport remains interrupted or employment has not returned.

Recovery planning therefore considers physical assets and the services and livelihoods those assets support.

Housing recovery

Housing recovery may involve temporary accommodation, repair of partially damaged dwellings and permanent reconstruction of destroyed homes. The appropriate approach depends on the severity of damage, local risks, land availability, household needs and applicable standards.

Repair restores a structure that can safely remain in use after appropriate work. Reconstruction creates a replacement when damage is too severe or a safer form of housing is required. Relocation may be considered where rebuilding in the original location would expose people to unacceptable risk, but it also raises questions about employment, schools, social networks, land rights and consent.

Safer housing recovery commonly requires:

  • Assessment of the safety and condition of existing buildings.
  • Compliance with applicable construction and land-use requirements.
  • Financial and technical support suited to household circumstances.
  • Consideration of tenants, people without secure tenure and persons with disabilities.
  • Access to water, sanitation, transport, health facilities and livelihoods.

A house is not fully recovered merely because a structure has been built. Safe habitation also depends on services, accessibility, affordability and a viable surrounding settlement.

Restoring essential infrastructure

Infrastructure includes the facilities and networks that support production and daily life. Economic infrastructure includes electricity, transport and communications. Social infrastructure includes services associated with health, education and housing.

Disaster damage to one network can affect several others. If electricity supply fails, water pumping and telecommunications may also be disrupted. If a bridge remains closed, patients may struggle to reach a hospital and farmers may be unable to take produce to market.

Recovery priorities should therefore reflect criticality, not merely the monetary value of the damaged asset. A comparatively inexpensive repair to the only access road may be more urgent than a costlier repair that affects fewer people.

Livelihood recovery

A livelihood includes the means through which individuals and households obtain income and meet their needs. Livelihood recovery may require replacing productive assets, restoring access to markets, restarting work and preventing a temporary income shock from becoming long-term poverty.

Affected livelihoodTypical disruptionPossible recovery measure
FarmingLoss of crops, inputs or access to irrigation.Restoration of agricultural inputs and irrigation services.
FisheriesDamaged boats, equipment or landing facilities.Repair of productive assets and market access.
Small businessDamaged premises, stock or interrupted customers.Support to reopen business and restore supply chains.
Wage employmentTemporary loss of work or reduced working days.Income support, temporary employment and access to new work.

Different households may need different assistance even within the same village. A fishing household may require equipment, while a wage worker may principally need temporary income support.

Integrating disaster risk reduction into reconstruction

Build Back Better requires recovery investments to account for the hazards that caused or intensified the earlier damage. Examples include safer siting of settlements, restoration of protective ecosystems, improved public-service continuity and suitable enforcement of safety standards.

Not every improvement is automatically a disaster mitigation measure. Spending must address an identified risk and be suitable for the local context. For instance, repairing a frequently flooded road without examining its exposure may recreate repeated future losses.

Reconstruction must also balance speed with safety. Rapid reopening of essential services is valuable, but permanent investment should not unnecessarily reproduce known vulnerabilities.

Prelims focus

  • Economic infrastructure: transport, energy and communications.
  • Social infrastructure: health, education and housing-related services.
  • Livelihood restoration may require income support as well as repair of productive assets.
  • Relocation must consider both physical safety and access to livelihoods and services.
  • Trap: Replacing damaged infrastructure in its original vulnerable condition is not necessarily Build Back Better.

[Sources: NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, chapter 8, Infrastructure, sections 8.2–8.3, printed pp. 140–141; World Bank, Safer Homes, Stronger Communities: A Handbook for Reconstructing after Natural Disasters, chapters on housing reconstruction and community participation (2010); UNDRR, Sendai Framework Terminology, entries Recovery, Reconstruction and Build Back Better (2017). Online sources consulted 2 November 2026.]
